Proposal


Show:

Further information:
Eddie Izzard in SA

Colourful UK comedian/actor/writer that many people know from his “cake or death” routine.


Eddie Izzard (54) is in South Africa running 27 marathons in 27 days for Sport Relief.

(Sport Relief is an off shoot of Comic Relief)
The comedian is planning the challenge to reflect the life of Nelson Mandela who served 27 years in prison in the county.

His route will trace Mandela’s life story; starting in his birthplace, before journeying to the school and university that he attended, then on to Cape Town and Robben Island where he was imprisoned.

He started running on the 23rd of February and has also visited organisation and communities that have been helped by Comic Relief.

He is near the end of the race now and hopes to finish at the Union Building on March 20th where Mandela gave his inaugural speech as the first democratically elected president of South Africa in 1994.

In 2012 Izzard attempted a similar feat but had to pull out for health reasons and the trek follows his 2009 challenge when he completed 43 marathons in 51 days across the UK to raise over £1.8 million.

The BBC has been following his race and there are weekly highlights of their run.We can have access to their footage.

Here is a link of week 1.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XcTx0ndK28I

While watching the link above you will see the lipstick and painted nails.
Izzard calls himself transgender but identifies as a straight man who likes women.
Here is the excerpt from wiki.
Izzard started to freely talk about his transvestism in venues like Edinburgh Festival as early as 1992.His stance is that cross-dressing is neither part of his performance nor a sexual fetish. He remarks in his show Unrepeatable, "Women wear what they want and so do I." According to Izzard, "Most transvestites fancy women."He identifies as "a straight transvestite or a male lesbian". He has also described himself as "a lesbian trapped in a man's body",transgender,and "a complete boy plus half girl”.




Locations:
Johannesburg

Press Release:


Eddie Izzard Marathon Man
Why is Eddie Izzard on the run in South Africa? Renowned for his cross-dressing habits and biting wit on stage, the comedian has just completed 27 marathons in 27 days. The staggering 1134km distance he’s run pays homage to the years Madiba spent in prison. He’s also raised millions for charity. Carte Blanche catches up with the so-called Marathon Man.


Script:


Eddie Izzard Script

V/O
Award winning transgender comic Eddie Izzard, is very comfortable on the big stage entertaining sold out audiences with his surreal sense of humour.

“I told people, I just couldn’t stop myself saying “I am playing at Wembley” and they go “At the Stadium?”, “No, the Arena” Laughter.

V/O
This is Mveso in the Eastern Cape, the birthplace of Nelson Mandela.

And Eddie is a little less assured of the challenge he has set himself. He is devoting 27 days to honour the 27 years that Madiba was imprisoned.

“I have to run 27 marathons in 27 days, from tomorrow, no days off, I tried it 4 years ago and I failed this time I must succeed, I think I can do it.”

V/O
It’s a daunting task for anyone. Eddie’s plan is to run from Mbashe Bridge in Mveso, to Cape Town and then fly to Pretoria and finish at Union Buildings where Mandela was inaugurated.

“This is sunrise this is Africa, let me get going. Cheers” carol put dates up on screen – DAY 1: DATE etc so we know when this is all happening.

V/O
He is running to places that were significant in Mandela’s life to raise money for Sport Relief, the sister organization of Comic Relief, a British charity that supports NGOs around the world.

Bongani
“Eddie what was it about Nelson Mandela that mad you think that a this was something you thought you could do, and that you wanted to do?”




Eddie
“Well people of South Africa and around the world they’ll know that Nelson Mandela had a great soul I think, to come out after 27 years without bitterness and stronger than he went in, I like his thinking and try to emulate that.”

V/O
Eddie’s quest would daunt any seasoned extreme athlete. A marathon is 42.2 kilometers long. The total distance that he has set out to run? An incredible 1139 kilometers. At 54 years old he has to be on the road every day for at least 6 hours, in scorching heat.

Eddie
“So 27 marathons in 27 days was a salute to the 27 years he was in prison , I thought that could work and some resonance and traction for average people in SA and UK around the world go OK nice salute to the great man.”

V/O
But will he make it? This is not the first time he has attempted this incredible feat.

Eddie
“In 2012, I attempted to run 27 marathons in 27 days on the 3rd marathon I started to pee brown coloured pee, so that happened on day 3 and that turned out to be rabdomyolosis where your muscles start shredding and going into your blood stream so we had to pack in the whole thing back in 2012, so now in 2016 hopefully today we won’t have that situation.”

V/O
It looked like history would repeat itself, with temperatures of over 35 degrees Celcius, Eddie’s body started to take strain.

“This is hard, hard, hard”


V/O
Eddie was determined to push through the physical pain, but his support crew were very concerned about his dehydration.

“It’s tough”.

V/O
On day 4, he was admitted to a hospital in East London.

Tony
“He’s dehydrating and that is where the problem lies, he’s had blood tests done again now and he is rehydrated and he is on a drip.”

V/O
But Eddie was determined to continue. The medical team monitored his body closely as he struggled to acclimatize.

“I’ve been in hospitals twice in 2 days, oh crap, it’s tough.”

V/O
Although he had lost a day of running, Eddie continued to soldier on. To avoid the heat and dehydration, his medical team suggested he run early mornings and late afternoons and they regularly monitored his vitals.

There was the occasional reprieve from the heat.

“A storm in Africa….at least it is cool.”

V/O
By avoiding the heat and maintaining a slow jog and steady walk,
Eddie’s body recovered and he was able to complete a marathon every day as planned.

“It’s a bear hug”

“So I am exhausted but it is good another marathon today.”

Bongani
“You are mostly known as a comedian or was the endurance and the sport aspect also a part of your life?”

Eddie
“Doing the big endurance runs was an idea that I came up with had for giving my health back to me, we are all natural animals , if you look at wild animals not one of them is unfit, not one single wild animal. Then we discovered sugar, refined sugar is really bad and we had cake and television and these things just took us into being these couch potatoes I’m trying to push against that.”

V/O
He didn’t train specifically for the marathons. He generally keeps fit, but mostly relied on his mental fortitude.

Half way through the 27 day challenge he has developed his own rhythm and his body has adapted to the taxing pace.

Sarah

“Physically you are able to see that his shape has changed, more muscle definition, legs more defined and generally looking stronger.”

Bongani
revoice
“Tell me about some significant moments for you on the route?”

Eddie
“Up in the Eastern Cape, meeting people up there, the local community, they looked at me, a white guy running along and they are going what is this guy. I have a SA flag and they are going that’s OK. And then I say Molo, ah molo, o molweni, kunjani, pilele, so I had a few lines there and I realized it changed their faces so I love that reaction.”

V/O
His journey touched the hearts of many South Africans who ran with him along the way, to give him moral support.

Eddie also had the opportunity to meet organizations that have been helped by Comic Relief and Sport Relief.

Since 1990 they have supported 200 projects in South Africa helping over 3 million people in difficult circumstances.

Bongani
“So you have raised in excess of 45 million Rand so far.”



Eddie
“That’s the wonderful thing. I had this theory that people want to see celebrities sweat. I am well known in the UK and little bit known here but if you are a celebrity you have to do something, but can you really do something not just I did a bit I went over there, actually put it together and make it happen”

V/O
And while he looks very comfortable in his running shoes, he is no stranger to stilettoes.

“I am here to get my nails fixed there is a broken one there….”

Bongani

‘As a public persona there are so many facets to who you are, I mean I am looking at your nails now and I know you have described yourself as a male lesbian. Can you tell me about that part of your persona?”

Eddie

“I am a transgender person. I have boy genetics and girl genetics, I think it is all genetics. Hasn’t been proved yet but pretty sure it is there, I knew whenI was 4 years old, I would wear dresses heels make up or wont. I’ll be in boy mode or girl mode, a bit like a super hero. I think it’s a gift to myself. That was the beginning of my mental training , my mental fortitude comes from the day 31 years ago when I walked out the door and I said I think this is honest and people are just going to have to get used to this.”

“Good to do a marathon with”.

V/O
From the start at Mveso in the Eastern, with close to a 1000 kms completed, Eddie arrived in Cape Town in high spirits.

“I like urban running.”

V/O
On day 24 Eddie ran around Robben Island, one of the most significant places in Mandela’s life.

“Days 24 Robben Island”

V/O
While he was running on the desolate island, he was reminded of one of Mandela’s quotes about courage.

“I learnt that courage was not the absence of fear but the triumph over fear, the brave man is not he who does not feel afraid but he who conquers that fear.”

Bongani
“You did get a chance to meet Nelson Mandela once?”

Eddie
“I did in 2010, I met Nelson Mandela, South Africa opened up to doing comedy here and people said you should come we know about your comedy I’ll come and do some shows and take the money and give it to him. And then we heard that he is going to meet you and that was odd because he had stopped meeting people he had a great energy and all of that vitality, he was how you would expect him to be, so that was great and I hope he would be pleased with what I have done.’

V/O
Eddie flew from Cape Town to Pretoria, to end the last leg of his journey at the statue of Nelson Mandela at the Union Buildings.

V/O
Having missed a day at the start of the challenge due to illness, Eddie gave everything to the last day of running and caught up the lost kilometers by doing two marathons – 84.4km – on his last day.

“I had to do two marathons in one day so that was the hardest day ever.”


“I’m struggling, really struggling.”

V/O
Eddie completed his quest: 27 marathons in 27 days, at the Union Buildings at the feet of Madiba whose outstretched arms symbolize his embrace of the whole nation.

“Nelson Mandela said don’t judge me by my successes judge me by the number of times I have failed and got back up again.

“27 Years, 27 Marathons”

Promo

1 x 15
Any seasoned extreme athlete would be fearful of running 27 marathons in 27 days, but British transgender Comic Eddie Izzard set himself the challenge to honour Mandela’s legacy.

It’s tough , It’s tough.

2 X 15

“I am going to run 27 marathons in 27 days.”

British comedian Eddie Izzard has run 1134 kilometers to honour Mandela and raise over 45 million Rand for the charity Sport Relief.

He is near the end of the race now and hopes to finish at the Union Building on March 20th where Mandela gave his inaugural speech as the first democratically elected president of South Africa in 1994. In 2012 Izzard attempted a similar feat but had to pull out for health reasons and the trek follows his 2009 challenge when he completed 43 marathons in 51 days across the UK to raise over £1.8 million. The BBC has been following his race and there are weekly highlights of their run.We can have access to their footage. Here is a link of week 1. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XcTx0ndK28I While watching the link above you will see the lipstick and painted nails. Izzard started to freely talk about his transvestism in venues like Edinburgh Festival as early as 1992.His stance is that cross-dressing is neither part of his performance nor a sexual fetish. He remarks in his show Unrepeatable, "Women wear what they want and so do I." According to Izzard, "Most transvestites fancy women."He identifies as "a straight transvestite or a male lesbian". He has also described himself as "a lesbian trapped in a man's body",transgender,and "a complete boy plus half girl”.
